title: Garage Sale

jokes.text: Oscar owns a large collection of Will & Grace merchandise/DVDs despite not being a fan — everyone assumes he is because he's gay
jokes.setup: Someone notices Oscar has Will & Grace items and assumes he's a big fan
jokes.punchline: "Nope. Everybody assumes I am. I always get them as gifts." — the joke is that Oscar's gay identity causes people to constantly gift him a show he doesn't actually like
jokes.explanation: A beautifully compressed character joke that opens the episode. The specificity of Will & Grace as the assumed gay-man's show, the deadpan delivery implied by 'Nope,' and the sad resignation of 'I always get them as gifts' pack enormous character insight into three short lines. It's very much an Oscar-only joke — no other character could deliver this. Economy is near-perfect.

jokes.text: "10 cents of every dollar is going into the party fund so we can throw parties for ourselves."
jokes.setup: Michael frames the garage sale as a generous communal event like many Americans do
jokes.punchline: The charity is actually just self-serving — they're funding their own parties
jokes.explanation: Classic Michael Scott obliviousness — the 'charity' is entirely circular and self-serving, and he says it with complete sincerity. The 'like many Americans' opener sets up a false gravitas that makes the deflation funnier. Solid character beat.

jokes.text: Extended argument over whether to leave the garage door open in the cold, with Dwight insisting the cold 'will drive business inside' and refusing to close it
jokes.setup: The garage door is open and it's cold; everyone wants it closed
jokes.punchline: Dwight has a pseudo-logical reason the cold is good for business and stubbornly refuses to close it, escalating into a childish standoff
jokes.explanation: Functional Dwight stubbornness comedy. His counter-logic ('The warmth will lure people inside') is characteristically absurd. The repetitive 'Close it. Close it. Stop it!' escalation is fine but not especially inventive. Pam's flat interjection to Kevin is a nice button.

jokes.text: "Schrutes are farmers by hobby and traders by trade." — Dwight announces his grand trading scheme starting with a used thumbtack
jokes.setup: Dwight spots a crooked sign and uses a thumbtack as an opening gambit in an elaborate trading scheme
jokes.punchline: His grandiose self-mythology ('Schrutes are farmers by hobby and traders by trade') is completely disproportionate to trading a thumbtack for a used candle
jokes.explanation: The aphorism 'Schrutes are farmers by hobby and traders by trade' is excellent Dwight mythology-building — it sounds like something handed down through generations and applied to the most trivial situation imaginable. High character integration; only Dwight would frame a garage sale thumbtack trade as ancestral destiny.

jokes.text: Dwight trades a thumbtack for a used candle by pointing out the crooked sign is 'trash, like your sign'
jokes.setup: Dwight offers a thumbtack to fix a crooked sign, then uses it as leverage
jokes.punchline: He insults the sign ('it looks awful / trash, like your sign') to lower the person's self-esteem and complete the trade — absurd negotiating tactic that works
jokes.explanation: Dwight's manipulative trading logic is consistently funny. The insult-as-negotiation is in character. 'That's how it's done' triumphant button on trading a thumbtack for a used candle is the best part.

jokes.text: Couple negotiating over a neon sign — price swings wildly, culminating in the revelation it might go into storage 'in case something changes'
jokes.setup: Jim and Pam haggle with a customer over a neon bar sign; Pam says she doesn't know why she brought it because 'it's kind of priceless'
jokes.punchline: Jim suggests putting it in storage 'in case,' and Pam's 'in case of what?' reveals the uncomfortable implication that Jim has a mental escape hatch from the marriage
jokes.explanation: The neon sign negotiation is funny on its face, but the real comedy comes from Jim's revealing 'in case' — a bachelor-pad relic he's not ready to release. The cringe cuts deeper than a surface joke. Pam's 'I don't have an in case. Do you have an in case?' in the confessional is the actual punchline, and it lands with understated menace.

jokes.text: Pam's confessional: "I don't have an 'in case.' Do you have an 'in case'?" — staring at the camera with barely concealed concern
jokes.setup: Jim's 'in case something changes' comment about the neon sign implies he has a mental escape hatch from their marriage
jokes.punchline: Pam's direct-to-camera rhetorical question reveals she's genuinely unsettled — the joke is the camera becoming a therapist she's accidentally venting to
jokes.explanation: This is a perfectly constructed talking-head beat. 'I don't have an in case. Do you have an in case?' is funny as a quote but devastating in context. It earns high marks for structure and character integration — Pam's barely-masked anxiety playing as comedy is very much The Office's wheelhouse. The economy is exceptional: nine words that contain an entire relationship concern.

jokes.text: Michael calls Holly's father, pretends he's going to fire Holly, then pivots to asking for her hand in marriage
jokes.setup: Michael calls Mr. Flax to ask his blessing for proposing to Holly
jokes.punchline: He opens with 'I'm going to have to fire your daughter Holly because she's such a terrible employee' before revealing it's a joke and pivoting to his actual request
jokes.explanation: Classic Michael: he cannot make a sincere phone call without first deploying an ill-advised prank. The misdirection (firing joke) followed by the earnest pivot to marriage intentions captures Michael's social dysfunction perfectly. The voicemail format makes it worse — he can't read the room because there is no room. Very well-integrated character comedy.

jokes.text: Dwight approaches Angela's table and tells her that a half-used candle signals to men that she's seeing someone else, making them 'lock her down fast'
jokes.setup: Dwight is trying to trade up his used candle and approaches Angela's spinster-ish table of tchotchkes
jokes.punchline: He delivers a pickup-artist-style 'negging' lecture about what the half-used candle signals to men — it's Dwight using absurd logic to manipulate Angela while also being weirdly perceptive about his own strategy
jokes.explanation: The joke works on multiple levels: Dwight is trading up while simultaneously running a bizarre seduction strategy on his secret ex. 'Spinster tchotchkes' is a great insult. The pickup-artist manipulation logic delivered completely straight is very Dwight. The layered relationship subtext earns the rewatch bonus.

jokes.text: Angela lets Dwight take her Helen Fielding and Jennifer Weiner collection — signaling she's giving up on romance
jokes.setup: Dwight's 'half-used candle' lecture implies Angela needs to project less romantic desperation
jokes.punchline: Angela surrenders her entire chick-lit romance novel collection, implying she's accepted her bleak romantic fate
jokes.explanation: A visual/contextual joke — the specific authors (Bridget Jones, chick-lit staples) communicate volumes about Angela's self-image and the sad resignation of giving them up. Works better on rewatch when you know the Dwight/Angela arc.

jokes.text: Andy proposes making the Dallas board game 'a little interesting' after Kevin reveals there are no instructions
jokes.setup: The group finds the Dallas board game has no instructions
jokes.punchline: Andy suggests making it 'interesting' — setting up the running gag of completely made-up, chaotic game rules
jokes.explanation: Functional setup for the Dallas running gag. The joke here is mostly anticipatory — funnier in retrospect once the chaotic game unfolds. On its own, modest.

jokes.text: "What is this? How did those get out? I'm sorry." — Jim embarrassed that his 'Professor Copperfield's Miracle Legumes' beans are on the table
jokes.setup: Jim discovers Pam has put something embarrassing of his out at the garage sale
jokes.punchline: The item is a packet of 'Professor Copperfield's Miracle Legumes' — magic beans — which Jim clearly bought sincerely and is now mortified about
jokes.explanation: The name 'Professor Copperfield's Miracle Legumes' is doing a lot of heavy lifting here and it lands. Jim's flustered 'How did those get out?' implies sincere shame, which is the joke — competent, skeptical Jim bought magic beans. The reaction beat and the absurdity of the beans' name are both well-executed.

jokes.text: Jim's story about buying magic beans in Jamaica from a man who 'told me things about myself that there's no way he could have known' — then the man vanished
jokes.setup: Jim explains the origin of 'Professor Copperfield's Miracle Legumes'
jokes.punchline: Jim — the show's resident straight man and skeptic — fully bought magic beans from a Jamaican stranger, tried to get a refund, and the man had vanished. He casually ends with 'So you want to sell me magic beans?'
jokes.explanation: The comedy of this moment hinges entirely on Jim being the one who fell for it. Jim is the show's audience surrogate — the rational one — and the revelation that he sincerely bought magic beans and even tried to get his money back (from a man who then disappeared) is a perfect character subversion. Dwight's 'That's a common swindler's trick' followed by Jim's casual 'Probably. Probably.' is impeccable timing.

jokes.text: "Correction. I do not want to sell you 'Professor Copperfield's Miracle Legumes.' Nice try. No, correction, terrible try."
jokes.setup: Dwight asks if Jim wants to sell him the magic beans
jokes.punchline: Jim's 'correction' formulation — aping Dwight's own speech pattern — and then self-correcting his 'nice try' to 'terrible try' shows Jim has completely absorbed the beans' value despite their absurdity
jokes.explanation: Jim using Dwight's 'Correction' speech tic is a lovely detail. But the real joke is 'Nice try. No, correction, terrible try' — Jim immediately walking back even a mild compliment because Dwight's attempt was genuinely bad. The economy is excellent: maximum information in minimum words.

jokes.text: Holly calls home and her father can't focus on the conversation — keeps referencing a TV program about India and forgetting Holly is in Pennsylvania
jokes.setup: Holly calls home after Michael called her dad, trying to find out what's happening
jokes.punchline: Her father is clearly suffering from cognitive decline — he thinks she's asking about a TV show, forgets she lives in Pennsylvania, and gets passed to mom — the darkly funny helplessness of adult children managing aging parents
jokes.explanation: The comedy here is dark — Holly's dad's confusion is clearly dementia-adjacent, and the show plays it for gentle, uncomfortable laughs. 'Oh! Which one's decaf?' as a non-sequitur button is the best moment. It's more poignant than funny, but it contextualizes Holly's later decision and earns its place.

jokes.text: 'Oh! Which one's decaf?' — Holly's mom's complete non-sequitur ending the phone call.
jokes.setup: Holly is having a serious emotional phone conversation about Michael's proposal intentions.
jokes.punchline: Her mom's attention snaps entirely away to coffee — 'Which one's decaf?' — completely undercutting the moment.
jokes.explanation: The sudden non-sequitur is perfectly timed and delivered. It's a great button for the phone call scene — three words that obliterate the emotional stakes and summarize the parents' complete inability to engage. The economy is nearly perfect.

jokes.text: Michael has gas on his hands and shoes from writing a fire message proposal and asks Pam to light it
jokes.setup: Michael is planning to write a fire message proposing to Holly
jokes.punchline: He has covered himself in gasoline and casually asks Pam to 'do the honors' of lighting it — the casual delivery of a genuinely dangerous situation
jokes.explanation: Michael's complete unawareness of the danger he's put himself in (gasoline on hands and shoes) combined with the cheery 'Do the honors, please?' is very much his character. Pam's deadpan pivot to stopping him works well as straight-woman foil.

jokes.text: "Michael, you've had two ideas today, and one of them was great and the other one was terrible. I am not in the mood for riddles, Pam."
jokes.setup: Pam tries to diplomatically stop Michael from lighting the fire message
jokes.punchline: Michael's 'I am not in the mood for riddles, Pam' — treating a completely clear statement as cryptic — is the joke. His inability to accept obvious feedback is perfect Michael.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best lines. 'I am not in the mood for riddles, Pam' is a perfect Michael Scott line — it's highly quotable, instantly character-specific, and beautifully structured. Pam's statement could not be clearer (one idea is great, one is terrible), and Michael's response treats it as an impossible puzzle while also revealing that he knows one idea is bad and just doesn't want to confront it. The economy is exceptional — nine words that capture Michael's entire psychology. Justifies the 8+ rating easily.

jokes.text: Ryan is selling his mom's pesto at the garage sale under false pretenses — he told her it was for a 'pesto party for all my friends'
jokes.setup: Ryan offers free samples of pesto, explaining his mom makes 'the best pesto in the world' and she always says it's 'just for family'
jokes.punchline: He reveals he tricked his mom into making 100 bottles' worth by inventing a 'pesto party' — now he's selling it at a garage sale for profit. 'Pesto party? Really?' is Phyllis's deadpan reaction.
jokes.explanation: Classic Ryan: the grandiose business scheme with maximum exploitation of personal relationships for minimum gain. Tricking his mom into making 100 bottles of pesto under the pretense of a 'pesto party' is delightfully specific and dark. Phyllis's dry 'Pesto party? Really?' is the perfect reaction-beat button.

jokes.text: Ryan confessional: "And Phyllis just had that 'mom look' I wanted."
jokes.setup: Ryan explains why he gave Phyllis a free sample
jokes.punchline: He specifically targeted Phyllis because she has the 'mom look' — reducing a colleague to a demographic prop for his pesto scam
jokes.explanation: The casual dismissiveness of 'Phyllis just had that mom look I wanted' is very Ryan — treating a human being as a focus group. Short, sharp, character-specific.

jokes.text: "You got this kosher certified?" / "No. I meant like, 'It's cool. It's kosher. It's all good.'"
jokes.setup: A customer asks if Ryan's mom's pesto is kosher certified
jokes.punchline: Ryan misunderstands 'kosher' as slang for 'cool/fine' — revealing he doesn't understand basic religious dietary concepts while also being exactly the kind of oblivious Ryan mistake
jokes.explanation: A tight wordplay joke perfectly suited to Ryan's character — he's so unserious about this enterprise that he doesn't even know what 'kosher' means in a business context. The double meaning of 'kosher' (certified vs. slang for 'fine') is well-deployed, and Ryan's confident misdefinition is consistent with his fraudster energy.

jokes.text: Ryan's confessional: 'Ryan, you have such an interesting mind. So creative. All these new business ideas and artistic projects.' — Ryan says this about himself in third person
jokes.setup: Ryan is describing how things are going
jokes.punchline: He's complimenting himself in the third person with the exact words a sycophantic colleague or fan would use — profound self-regard deployed without irony
jokes.explanation: Ryan complimenting himself in third person using the exact language of a PR puff piece is a perfect encapsulation of his narcissism. 'All these new business ideas and artistic projects' — none of which we ever see amount to anything — lands well as character satire.

jokes.text: "Why would I want some random black man's old photo album sitting on my bookshelf? I'm not James Franco."
jokes.setup: Ryan has Stanley's old photo album and is considering throwing it away
jokes.punchline: His reason for not wanting it is that he's not James Franco — implying James Franco specifically collects random strangers' photo albums, or that James Franco has this kind of edgy-ironic aesthetic, and Ryan does not
jokes.explanation: This is a sharp, weird joke. The James Franco reference works because it perfectly captures a specific type of ironic-hipster aesthetic — collecting random strangers' memorabilia as an art project — and Ryan's rejection of it despite his own hipster pretensions is deeply funny. It's also a bit dark given the 'random black man' framing which makes it slightly edgy. The joke is genuinely original and quotable.

jokes.text: Dwight's confessional trading chain: 'thumb tack → Meredith's junk → Kelly's crap → Phyllis's garbage → Oscar's trash → Stanley's crap → Ryan's junk → Creed's garbage → a very cute squid that Erin happened to have'
jokes.setup: Dwight began his trading scheme with a thumbtack
jokes.punchline: The entire chain of trades uses synonyms for 'worthless junk' (junk, crap, garbage, trash) until arriving at the absurd and unexpected 'a very cute squid that Erin happened to have'
jokes.explanation: The structure of this joke is elegant: rotating synonyms for garbage (junk/crap/garbage/trash/crap/junk/garbage) creates a comedic rhythm, and 'a very cute squid that Erin happened to have' is the perfect absurdist button. 'That Erin happened to have' — as if possessing a squid is unremarkable — is the best part. Dwight's journalistic precision about his pointless trades is very in character.

jokes.text: Jim's reaction beat: 'Jim, put those away.' — Jim is embarrassed again about something at the garage sale (the beans reappearing or another embarrassing item)
jokes.setup: Pam tells Jim to put something away
jokes.punchline: The joke is Jim's presumed mortified look — the beans are back out, and Jim's carefully maintained cool-guy image is again undone by his own purchase
jokes.explanation: A running gag callback to the beans embarrassment. Functional but lighter than the original — it's the echo of a better joke. Works as a beat but doesn't add much.

jokes.text: Jim confessional: 'I'm really sorry. Pam must've put those out.' / 'What were the claims for those beans?' — Jim immediately starts justifying the beans' worth to Dwight
jokes.setup: Dwight catches Jim with the magic beans again and asks about their claimed properties
jokes.punchline: Jim, who was previously embarrassed, pivots to defensively protecting the beans' mystique — 'You're just going to make fun of me, so why would I...' — fully invested in the beans despite his mortification
jokes.explanation: The comedy here is Jim's escalating investment in the beans — he was embarrassed they were out, but now he won't share their claims because Dwight 'will just make fun.' Jim's self-awareness is crumbling. It's well-structured as a character arc within a runner.

jokes.text: "You know what? This ends now." — Jim presumably decides to demonstrate the beans, followed by a scene break implying something absurd happened
jokes.setup: Jim won't tell Dwight the beans' claims because Dwight will make fun of him
jokes.punchline: Jim's sudden defiant 'This ends now' — followed by a cut — implies he's going to do something embarrassing with the beans to prove their worth
jokes.explanation: The cut after 'This ends now' does the comedy work — we don't see what Jim does, which is often funnier. The implication is he tested or demonstrated the beans in some way. The scene break is a visual/structural comedy tool well-used here.

jokes.text: Michael calls a meeting ostensibly about 'recycling' — but it's really about the proposal; he's forgotten he called it
jokes.setup: Everyone is summoned to the conference room for a Michael meeting
jokes.punchline: Michael has no idea why they're there and improvises 'I would like to talk to you today about recycling' — a completely irrelevant topic — before being redirected to the actual point
jokes.explanation: Classic Michael: he called a meeting but doesn't remember why, so he improvises with whatever word comes to mind — 'recycling.' The beat is fast and well-observed. Michael's 'I could not agree with you more' to himself when Dwight says 'we are a family' shows his wandering self-agreement.

jokes.text: Jim's proposal advice: 'If you are in a costume, you did something wrong. If at any point you find yourself tying the ring to a dog's collar, stop and look at yourself.'
jokes.setup: Jim offers Michael guidelines for how NOT to propose
jokes.punchline: The specificity of 'costume' and 'tying the ring to a dog's collar' implies these are based on things Michael has actually suggested — Jim's deadpan delivery makes it funnier
jokes.explanation: This is excellent comedy writing. The joke works because Jim's 'rules' are so specific that they imply a history of terrible proposals Michael has either attempted or pitched. 'Stop and look at yourself' is the perfect instruction — not 'don't do it' but 'pause and reflect on your choices.' Both examples (costume, dog collar) are vivid and specific. Highly quotable, great structure. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Kevin plays a 'blackmail card' and 'proxy meeting card' in the same turn in Dallas board game; Andy says you can't do both
jokes.setup: The group is playing Dallas board game with completely made-up rules
jokes.punchline: Kevin makes two power moves in one turn; Andy protests; Kevin's defense is that 'somebody forgot to staple the rule book to the inside of the game, like a normal human being'
jokes.explanation: Kevin's indignant 'like a normal human being' directed at whoever failed to staple the rulebook is a nice character beat — his outrage is misplaced given that he's the one making up nonsense rules. The escalation of the game chaos is well-paced.

jokes.text: Andy plays a 'share the wealth' card from The Game of Life — 'It was in the box.'
jokes.setup: The Dallas game has no rules so players are making them up freely
jokes.punchline: Andy produces a card from a completely different board game (The Game of Life), arguing it's valid because 'it was in the box' — and after brief protest, everyone agrees to honor it
jokes.explanation: The escalation to using a card from a different game entirely is a perfectly timed comedic peak. 'It was in the box' as a complete philosophical justification for cross-game card legitimacy is absurdist in the best way. 'We must honorably adhere to the rules that we are making up on the spot' is a great button that acknowledges the absurdity while doubling down.

jokes.text: "We must honorably adhere to the rules that we are making up on the spot."
jokes.setup: Someone protests the cross-game card rule as unfair
jokes.punchline: Andy's solemn declaration that they must honor rules they are simultaneously inventing — the meta-absurdity of the situation collapsed into one perfect sentence
jokes.explanation: This line is genuinely exceptional in its self-aware absurdism. The contradiction is stated plainly and seriously: 'we must honorably adhere to the rules that we are making up on the spot.' It's the perfect encapsulation of how arbitrary systems gain legitimacy through collective agreement, delivered as pure comedy. Highly quotable, near-perfect economy. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Darryl: 'No, but that's not fair.' Andy: 'Well, that's Dallas.' Darryl: 'Dallas indeed.'
jokes.setup: Darryl protests the cross-game card rule
jokes.punchline: 'Well, that's Dallas' / 'Dallas indeed' — the complete acceptance of the absurd as just how Dallas works, delivered with mock gravitas
jokes.explanation: 'That's Dallas' / 'Dallas indeed' is the perfect button on the board game sequence. The mock gravity of 'Dallas indeed' as an acceptance of complete nonsense is excellent. These four words are doing massive comedic work. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Stanley recognizes his own photo album in Ryan's garage sale pile
jokes.setup: Ryan was considering throwing out 'some random black man's old photo album'
jokes.punchline: That man is Stanley, who presumably finds his own memories being sold at a garage sale — the callback payoff of Ryan's earlier dismissal
jokes.explanation: The payoff of Ryan's earlier dismissal ('Why would I want some random black man's old photo album') landing on the actual man (Stanley) is a clean visual callback. Stanley's 'What? Ryan, where did you get this picture?' is the implied line. Works well as a structural joke.

jokes.text: Ryan's confessional: 'My mom also makes the best salsa.' — completely unprompted pivot after the Stanley confrontation
jokes.setup: Ryan has just been caught selling Stanley's family photos
jokes.punchline: He pivots immediately to pitching his mom's salsa — no acknowledgment of the awkwardness, pure shameless salesmanship
jokes.explanation: The absolute shamelessness of pivoting from being caught selling a colleague's family photos to 'My mom also makes the best salsa' is pitch-perfect Ryan. No transition, no acknowledgment, pure hustle. The economy is exceptional — it's seven words that contain an entire character.

jokes.text: Holly's confessional about when to move a parent to care: 'If you wait for the day when your parent comes to you and says, "I can't take care of myself," that's never going to happen.'
jokes.setup: Holly is discussing her father's cognitive decline and the question of when to make a care decision
jokes.punchline: The dark truth that aging parents will never admit their own incapacity — delivered straight but landing as grim, rueful comedy
jokes.explanation: More observational-dark than outright funny, but it's a real insight delivered with economy and a kind of rueful wisdom that earns its laugh. Phyllis's non-sequitur 'I have a box of bras under the table if you're interested' immediately after is the actual punchline — tonal whiplash that works.

jokes.text: "I have a box of bras under the table if you're interested." — Phyllis interjects into Holly's emotional moment
jokes.setup: Holly is having an emotional, vulnerable conversation about her father's cognitive decline
jokes.punchline: Phyllis completely ignores the emotional register and pivots to selling bras — the tonal whiplash is the joke
jokes.explanation: This line is a masterpiece of tonal juxtaposition. Phyllis's complete obliviousness to the emotional weight of Holly's confession and her pivot to 'a box of bras under the table' is perfectly timed. The specificity of 'under the table' makes it funnier — she's been sitting on this inventory the whole time. High economy, great structure. Justifies the 8 impact score.

jokes.text: Michael's proposal idea: throw a corpse dressed like him off the roof, head pops off, saying 'I lost my head when I fell in love with you'
jokes.setup: The group is brainstorming safe proposal ideas for Michael
jokes.punchline: Michael's suggestion involves a prop corpse, decapitation, and a pun — delivered with complete enthusiasm and the note 'Easy enough to get a corpse. You just go to a med school.'
jokes.explanation: This is Michael at his most Michael: a proposal idea that involves death, a pun, and complete logistical confidence. 'Easy enough to get a corpse. You just go to a med school.' is the escalating button that makes it great — his casualness about corpse procurement is the funniest part. 'I lost my head when I fell in love with you' as the payoff line he's clearly been workshopping shows his complete sincerity. High character integration.

jokes.text: Michael reveals the ring — 'They say three-year salary' — and everyone reacts with shock
jokes.setup: Michael is pitching elaborate proposal ideas, and someone says he doesn't need the corpse if he already has the ring
jokes.punchline: The ring is enormous — 'They say three-year salary' — delivered with Michael's complete sincerity about the guideline
jokes.explanation: The three-year salary joke is a good Michael beat — his literal interpretation of the 'guideline' and apparent ability to afford it (despite his regional manager salary) lands well. The group's collective 'EXCLAIMS' reaction implies it's visually stunning.

jokes.text: Pam says Jim proposed 'at a gas station' — the group is incredulous
jokes.setup: Pam tells Michael that Jim's proposal was perfect and simple — he got down on one knee and told her he loved her
jokes.punchline: Location reveal: 'At a gas station.' Everyone laughs. Jim then explains it was 'halfway between both of us' which somehow makes it more romantic and funnier simultaneously
jokes.explanation: The gas station reveal is a great subversion of the sentimental setup — Pam builds it up as perfect and romantic, and the location is a gas station. The additional layer of 'it was halfway between both of us' recontextualizes it as both practical and genuinely sweet, which makes it funnier by being earnest. Jim and Pam's relationship is so well-established that the gas station becoming romantic feels earned.

jokes.text: Michael: 'That must have been a surprise when at the gas station you proposed.' Jim: 'No, it was really sweet. It was raining.' Michael: 'Yeah, you didn't say that the weather was bad.'
jokes.setup: Michael asks Jim about the gas station proposal
jokes.punchline: Michael's response to learning it was raining — 'Yeah, you didn't say that the weather was bad' — treats rain as a disqualifying flaw while Jim sees it as romantic. Classic Michael missing the point while being technically correct
jokes.explanation: Michael's 'you didn't say that the weather was bad' is excellent — it's a completely literal reading that exposes his romantic naivety. He can't conceive of rain as romantic because he takes things at face value. The delivery ('Yeah, you didn't say that the weather was bad') sounds like he's checking off a complaint form. High character integration.

jokes.text: Michael: 'I want this to be an event that everyone talks about always and forever.' Jim: 'Totally reasonable.'
jokes.setup: Michael states his proposal ambitions
jokes.punchline: Jim's flat 'Totally reasonable' — delivered with perfect straight-faced sarcasm as Michael's demands are clearly insane
jokes.explanation: Jim's deadpan validation of Michael's insane ambitions is reliable Office comedy. 'Totally reasonable' is doing ironic heavy lifting in two words. Functional and well-delivered but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Kevin confessional: 'Get this. Kevin thought I was going to sell my Bowflex for $200. And I told him, "Dude, this was a prop in my movie."'
jokes.setup: Kevin is recounting a garage sale negotiation about his Bowflex exercise machine
jokes.punchline: Kevin refers to himself in the third person ('Kevin thought') and casually reveals the Bowflex was a prop in his movie — the absurdity is that Kevin has apparently made a movie, and this fact is delivered as if completely normal
jokes.explanation: Kevin referring to himself in the third person is funny on its own. 'This was a prop in my movie' — delivered with complete casualness — is the real joke. We get no context for Kevin's movie and that's exactly right. High character integration; this level of oblivious self-importance is peak Kevin.

jokes.text: Holly begins to propose to Michael — 'Michael Scott, will you...' — and Michael panics and shuts it down
jokes.setup: Holly is about to propose to Michael — she's been building to asking him to go to Colorado with her and perhaps marry her
jokes.punchline: Michael immediately panics: 'No, no. Shut it.' / 'Oh God, nope, nope, nope.' — he doesn't want to be proposed to in the break room
jokes.explanation: This is a brilliant subversion: Holly is proposing to Michael, but Michael refuses because 'that is not going to be our story.' His refusal isn't reluctance to marry her — it's that he's already planned something better and won't let her steal his moment. 'Should have burned this place down when I had a chance' is a perfect dark button that references his longstanding feelings about the office. Excellent character integration — only Michael would do this.

jokes.text: "Should have burned this place down when I had a chance."
jokes.setup: Michael has just rejected Holly's proposal attempt in the break room
jokes.punchline: His muttered 'Should have burned this place down when I had a chance' — referencing his longstanding hatred of the office while also being genuinely unhinged as a response to being proposed to
jokes.explanation: Six words that are among the episode's best. 'Should have burned this place down when I had a chance' is a genuinely great line — darkly funny, character-specific, and completely unhinged as a romantic response. It also implies he had a previous 'chance' to burn it, which is both alarming and hilarious. Highly quotable. The economy is near-perfect. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Kevin's Dallas endgame: 'Hey, guys, it's my turn.' / 'You can't go. You're dead. I shot you five moves ago.'
jokes.setup: The Dallas game has devolved into total chaos with made-up rules
jokes.punchline: Kevin doesn't acknowledge that he's been dead for five moves — he just wants his turn. The logic of the game has fully collapsed.
jokes.explanation: Kevin insisting on his turn despite having been dead for five moves is good Kevin comedy. 'I start having rules now, everything we've built collapses' is an excellent line from whoever delivers it — the logic of protecting an illegitimate system is perfectly absurd.

jokes.text: 'Should have burned this place down when I had a chance.' — Michael's aside after stopping Holly's proposal.
jokes.setup: Michael has just thwarted Holly's break room proposal because it's not romantic enough.
jokes.punchline: His dark aside about burning the building implies a long-standing fantasy of office destruction, treated as casually as complaining about the coffee.
jokes.explanation: A great throwaway that works precisely because it's not explained. Michael's casual dark thought about arson, dropped into a romantic moment, is vintage Michael Scott absurdism. The brevity is perfect — it's funnier for not being dwelt upon.

jokes.text: "I start having rules now, everything we've built collapses."
jokes.setup: Andy is defending the lawless state of the Dallas game against Kevin's demands for rules
jokes.punchline: The sentence acknowledges that their 'system' is built entirely on chaos and would be destroyed by any principled standard — yet he defends it as an achievement
jokes.explanation: This line works as a perfect absurdist statement about corrupt systems — the entire framework exists only if you never question it. 'Everything we've built collapses' treats their nonsense game as a civilization-scale achievement. It's highly quotable and structurally excellent. Earns its 8 on originality — this is a surprisingly smart joke embedded in a silly board game sequence.

jokes.text: Darryl's button on the Dallas sequence: 'And that is Dallas.'
jokes.setup: The Dallas game has ended in chaos, recriminations, and demands for money back
jokes.punchline: Darryl delivers the running catchphrase one final time — 'And that is Dallas' — with full deadpan gravitas, as if summarizing a profound lesson
jokes.explanation: The final 'And that is Dallas' lands better than the earlier iteration because it's the button on the entire arc. Darryl's deadpan delivery gives it gravitas it absolutely doesn't deserve, which is exactly the joke. Economy of 9.5 — four words that close out a full running gag.

jokes.text: Jim and Ryan plant the magic beans in a pot and something appears to have grown — 'That's impossible. It is, right? I mean, it's impossible.'
jokes.setup: Jim has been defending and protecting the magic beans throughout the episode
jokes.punchline: After planting them, something appears to have sprouted — the joke is that the beans might actually be magic, or at least Jim and Ryan can't deny that something grew. Jim's 'All right. I'll take them.' validates his original belief.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best joke structurally. The entire magic beans runner has been building to this payoff: Jim was embarrassed, then defensive, then secretive, and now the beans appear to have actually worked. The show doesn't confirm it — 'That's impossible. It is, right? I mean, it's impossible.' — leaving the viewer in the same uncertain state as Jim. Jim's 'All right. I'll take them. They're probably worthless. Probably.' is the perfect half-conviction. The episode then rewards this by having Dwight trade the telescope for the beans, validating Jim's intuition through Dwight's legendary trader instincts. Multi-layered, beautifully structured over 11 minutes, earns its ending completely.

jokes.text: Dwight trades the telescope for the magic beans — 'They're probably worthless. Probably.' / 'Leave the telescope.'
jokes.setup: Dwight has successfully traded from a thumbtack all the way up to a telescope
jokes.punchline: He immediately trades the telescope back for the magic beans — undoing his entire day's work for something he just witnessed do something impossible
jokes.explanation: The perfect anti-climax and the episode's best callback payoff. Dwight has spent the entire episode trading up from a thumbtack, achieved a telescope, and then immediately surrenders it all for magic beans — completing the Jack and the Beanstalk fairy tale arc. 'Probably worthless. Probably.' is a great concession of doubt. 'Leave the telescope' is the confident reversal. Excellent structure, strong character integration — Dwight's obsessive nature driving him to acquire the impossible thing rather than the merely impressive thing.

jokes.text: Dwight's confessional: he started with a thumb tack, traded up to a telescope, then traded the telescope back for the beans — 'In a way the most valuable thing here wasn't the telescope at all. No. It was this packet of beans.'
jokes.setup: Dwight has been trading all episode, reaching a telescope as his peak item
jokes.punchline: He trades the telescope — the 'best' item — back for the magic beans, because Dwight recognizes their value. His completely straight delivery of 'I can just go buy another telescope' as if this is obvious makes it land.
jokes.explanation: This is the payoff of two separate runners (Dwight's trading scheme and Jim's magic beans) that converge in the most satisfying way. Dwight, the master trader, validates Jim's irrational faith in the beans by recognizing their worth — 'I can just go buy another telescope' is the perfect Dwight logic. The joke works because Dwight's legendary pragmatism endorses something completely absurd. High character integration for both characters involved. The structural elegance of two B-plots resolving together earns 9.0 structure and earned_vs_cheap.

jokes.text: Holly and Michael's garage sale results: 'Thirteen dollars. That's great. And still have most of our stuff? Good.'
jokes.setup: The garage sale is over and they're tallying results.
jokes.punchline: They've made $13 and sold almost nothing — Michael calls this 'great,' which is a hilariously low bar that he's completely satisfied with.
jokes.explanation: Quick joke that lands because of Michael's completely unearned enthusiasm. $13 being 'great' is a funny data point. Not a standout but earns its place.

jokes.text: Michael's tour of meaningful office locations: 'This is where Toby announced he was going to Costa Rica. It was the happiest day of my life until the day you came to replace him.'
jokes.setup: Michael is taking Holly on a sentimental tour of their relationship's meaningful locations in the office
jokes.punchline: The first 'meaningful place' is meaningful because of Toby leaving — Michael's hatred of Toby is so profound that Toby's announced departure is a top-two life highlight
jokes.explanation: This is a nearly perfect Michael Scott joke. He's trying to be romantic and sentimental, and the very first location is significant because of his hatred of Toby. 'It was the happiest day of my life until the day you came to replace him' is exquisitely structured — it's simultaneously romantic (Holly is now his happiest day) and deranged (because Toby hatred ranks). High character integration, highly quotable. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Michael: 'I was sitting at this desk when I called you to tell you that I had herpes and that I was still in love with you, and you said it was over... But thank goodness none of that was true, including the herpes. Ingrown hair.'
jokes.setup: Michael is recounting a pivotal moment in their relationship — a painful phone call where Holly rejected him
jokes.punchline: The herpes reveal: Michael told Holly he had herpes (as a way to reconnect?) and then clarifies it was an ingrown hair. The casual 'including the herpes. Ingrown hair.' is the perfect button.
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional. 'Thank goodness none of that was true, including the herpes. Ingrown hair.' is a stunning line. The pivot from romantic vulnerability to herpes disclosure to immediate medical clarification ('Ingrown hair.') delivered deadpan in a moment of emotional intimacy is peak Michael Scott. It's highly quotable, perfectly structured, and could only be said by Michael. The two-word button 'Ingrown hair.' delivered as a standalone sentence is a small masterpiece of comic timing. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Michael recounts the 'obesity awareness' meeting they co-ran: 'Saved a lot of lives that day. That's when you first met Michael Klump. "I say, I say, I'll sit on you."'
jokes.setup: Michael is recounting the early days of their relationship, including a meeting they co-ran
jokes.punchline: Michael Klump — his obese alter ego character — is referenced with a catchphrase impression. Holly laughing confirms this is a shared memory. The absurdity of 'Saved a lot of lives that day' for an obesity awareness meeting is the secondary joke.
jokes.explanation: Works best for longtime viewers who remember Michael Klump. 'Saved a lot of lives that day' for an obesity awareness meeting in a paper company is peak Michael grandiosity. The impression callback ('I say, I say, I'll sit on you') is fan service that lands warmly.

jokes.text: Holly: 'That's when you first met Michael Klump.' Michael: 'I say, I say, I'll sit on you.' (Both laugh)
jokes.setup: They're recalling their shared history; Michael Klump was Michael's obese alter-ego character from the obesity awareness meeting.
jokes.punchline: Michael immediately does the Michael Klump voice — 'I say, I say, I'll sit on you' — and Holly loves it, which shows how uniquely matched they are.
jokes.explanation: The Michael Klump reference is a show-mythology callback that rewards longtime viewers. The fact that Holly laughs at it — where most people find Michael's characters mortifying — reinforces why they're perfect for each other. The character integration here is about the relationship dynamic, not just individual character. Gets a rewatch bonus for the emotional resonance.

jokes.text: Michael reminds Holly: 'Over there, that's where you realized that Meredith was prostituting herself for Outback steak. And you had the cutest look on your face because you couldn't believe it.'
jokes.setup: Michael is pointing out meaningful locations in the office tour
jokes.punchline: One of the 'meaningful' spots is where Holly learned about Meredith's prostitution-for-steak scheme — and Michael frames it as a tender shared memory, focused on Holly's 'cutest look'
jokes.explanation: The comedy of Michael framing 'learning about your colleague's sex work' as a tender relationship milestone is excellent. 'You had the cutest look on your face because you couldn't believe it' — Michael reading Holly's horror as charming disbelief is very in character. Rewards viewers who remember the original episode.

jokes.text: Michael reveals a spot that's just... a window he'd stand at to stare at Holly. 'I would just find an excuse to come here so I could stare at you through that window. This is what I'd do.'
jokes.setup: Michael has been pointing out meaningful shared milestones; Holly asks 'What happened here?'
jokes.punchline: 'Nothing, really. I would just find an excuse to come here so I could stare at you through that window.' The creepiness-as-romance framing is the joke — this is objectively stalker behavior delivered as pure sentiment
jokes.explanation: The joke hinges on Michael's complete unawareness that 'I used to find excuses to stare at you through a window' is creepy — he says it with pure romantic sincerity. Holly's reaction (apparently touched) makes it even funnier. Good character integration.

jokes.text: Michael asks every person in the annex to marry him; each one says 'No' in turn — 'That marriage would be a sham.' / 'That would be hot. I would pay to see that.'
jokes.setup: Michael enters the annex and begins his proposal — 'Holly, will you marry me?'
jokes.punchline: Every person in the room gets a proposal and declines with character-specific commentary — the escalation of rejections, each with a different flavor, building to Holly
jokes.explanation: This sequence is beautifully constructed. Michael proposes to everyone in the room before reaching Holly, each 'No' getting a distinct character-specific response: 'That marriage would be a sham' (Toby — implying contempt), 'Easy no' (someone dismissive), 'That would be hot. I would pay to see that' (likely Meredith). The escalation structure is clean, and 'Only one that I was kind of worried about' as the button before Holly is excellent. The sequence uses the full ensemble for maximum comedic payoff.

jokes.text: Michael's proposal: 'This is where I fell in love with you. And this is where I ask you to marry me.' — the candles spell out something, fire alarm goes off mid-proposal
jokes.setup: Michael has set up candles to spell a message as part of his proposal
jokes.punchline: The fire alarm triggers mid-proposal — the same fire-related risk Pam warned him about earlier — but Michael and Holly laugh through it, making the accidental chaos part of the romantic moment
jokes.explanation: The callback to Michael's earlier fire proposal idea pays off — he did use fire, and it did cause an alarm, but it doesn't ruin the moment. The irony that Pam was right AND it didn't matter is sweet. The chaos becoming romantic is a character beat for Michael and Holly.

jokes.text: "Holly Flax, marrying me, will you be?" / "Your wife becoming, be will I."
jokes.setup: Michael and Holly are laughing through the fire alarm chaos during the proposal
jokes.punchline: Michael does a Yoda-voice scrambled proposal; Holly responds in kind — their shared absurd humor language is the romantic payoff
jokes.explanation: This is the emotional and comedic peak of the episode. The Yoda-inverted proposal ('marrying me, will you be?') is perfectly Michael — even in his most sincere moment he can't resist a bit. Holly's matching response ('Your wife becoming, be will I') is the ideal payoff because it shows she loves him for exactly this: they share the same absurd romantic language. It's funny, sweet, and completely character-specific. Could not be delivered by any other two characters in any other show. Justifies 8.5+ on all metrics.

jokes.text: Michael announces 'we're moving to Colorado. All of us?' / 'Yep.' — the office's horrified reaction
jokes.setup: Michael announces his engagement to Holly and that they're moving to Colorado
jokes.punchline: Someone asks 'All of us?' and Michael says 'Yep' — Michael either doesn't understand or is trolling the entire office about them relocating
jokes.explanation: The final joke of the episode — Michael's trollish 'Yep' in response to 'All of us?' lands as a classic Michael misdirection. The clarification ('Holly has to go back to Colorado. I'm going with her. I'm leaving.') turns the joke into something genuinely emotional. Good button on the episode.

jokes.text: Michael announces to the group: 'We're moving to Colorado. All of us?' — the office's panic/confusion at Michael's announcement.
jokes.setup: Michael announces his engagement and that he's leaving for Colorado.
jokes.punchline: Someone asks 'All of us?' — which implies they genuinely thought Michael was moving the whole office, consistent with Michael's worldview that they are a family who does everything together.
jokes.explanation: A good button for the episode — the 'all of us?' reaction is funny because it's plausible given Michael's family-obsessed worldview. The implication is that this is the beginning of Michael's departure arc, and the comedy is tinged with something more emotional. The joke lands in the confusion of the reaction beats.

tmdb_overview: The office holds a garage sale in the warehouse. Michael decides to propose to Holly, and runs into trouble thinking of how to do it well.
